name: Greaser style

card.summary: The 1950s working-class youth look of greased-back hair, leather jackets, white tees and cuffed denim, used today as a retro style that sharpens a man's silhouette and grooming.
card.note: The term was historically used as a slur for poor laborers of Italian, Greek or Mexican descent.

quick.overview:
Greaser style comes from the greaser youth subculture of the 1950s and early 1960s in the United States and Canada. Its signature elements are slicked-back, pomaded hair, a leather or denim jacket, a plain white or black T-shirt, and dark cuffed jeans with boots [1].

Today people borrow it as a clean retro look: the hair gives a groomed, structured head shape, and the jacket-and-tee outfit is a simple way to look put together.
quick.how: The look is built around pomade or petroleum jelly to comb hair back into a pompadour or similar shape, with a Perfecto-style motorcycle jacket, white tee, rolled-cuff Levi's and engineer or work boots [1][2].
quick.risks: Heavy petroleum-based hair products need regular washing. Pomade is a styling product with no notable health risks beyond scalp reactions in some users.

lead: Greaser style is the clothing and grooming look of the greaser subculture, a working-class youth scene in the US and Canada that was established by the 1950s and remained prominent into the mid-1960s [1]. The look is greased-back hair, a leather or denim jacket, plain T-shirts, and cuffed denim with boots.

Men copied rock and roll figures such as Elvis Presley and Little Richard, wearing the pompadour and the duck's ass cut styled with pomade or petroleum jelly [1]. Women backcombed hair and wore leather jackets and cropped pants [1].
The look has been spread through film and television, including The Wild One (1953), Grease, The Outsiders, and Happy Days' Fonzie, and returned in a 1950s nostalgia wave from the mid-1970s [1].

chain: Pomade shapes hair into a slick pompadour or back-comb
Jacket, white tee and dark denim form a clean silhouette
angle.text: Followers use pomade-styled hair and a leather-jacket outfit as a recognisable, groomed style. The hairstyle gives the head a defined shape, and the outfit is simple to assemble.

infobox: Leather jacket, white tee, cuffed jeans, boots [1]

paras: Hair was styled with pomade or petroleum jelly and combed frequently. Men wore work pants, dark slacks or cuffed dark Levi's with engineer, combat, work or cowboy boots, plain T-shirts, and denim or leather jackets, including Perfecto motorcycle jackets [1]. Pomade is a greasy, waxy or water-based product that gives a slick shine and long hold, and is the traditional product for greased-back styles [2].

The subculture may have grown from post-World War II motorcycle clubs and 1940s street gangs, and Italian Americans, Mexican American Chicanos and other Hispanic youth were prominent members [1]. The word greaser was used in the late 1800s as a slur for poor laborers of Italian, Greek or Mexican descent, and the name also referred to the hair [1]. A backlash in the early 1960s promoted cleaner-cut acts, and by the mid-1970s the style was part of a nostalgia revival [1].

Pomades were most popular from the 1920s to the 1950s, with Dixie Peach a favorite of American teens from World War II through the 1960s, and the pompadour was popular from the mid-1950s to 1964 [2]. Pomade use returned in the 2010s alongside the undercut [2].

timeline.event: The Wild One becomes the first major film portrayal of the look [1].
S. E. Hinton's The Outsiders portrays a greaser gang [1].
Grease film released, part of the 1950s nostalgia revival [1].
